query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled pre-oxidation treatment that forms a thin, continuous, and adherent oxide (enriched in easily oxidizable elements like Cr and Cu) on the surface of a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating will increase wear resistance and promote more homogenous microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding by acting as a load‐bearing tribolayer and reducing local stress concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating produced by conventional deposition methods with minimal pre-formed surface oxides.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation treatment (e.g., thermal annealing in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere) to form a nano-scale, continuous oxide layer on the coating surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding tests performed in an ambient or controlled oxidizing environment at 600–800°C under typical contact loads; the pre-oxidation treatment might be conducted at ~700°C for a short duration in an O2/Ar mixture to achieve the desired oxide film.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanometer-thick, continuous oxide (tribolayer) that adheres well to the underlying HEA coating, reducing direct metal-metal contact during sliding.
generation.mechanism: The pre-formed oxide layer acts as a protective, load-bearing medium that reduces friction-induced stress concentrations and suppresses severe strain localization; this facilitates more uniform plastic deformation in the underlying alloy while the oxide itself endures sliding wear, thereby reducing overall material loss.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the untreated (baseline) coating, the pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coating is expected to exhibit reduced macroscopic wear (lower wear volume and improved friction coefficient) and show more homogeneously distributed microscopic deformation (smaller, evenly distributed plastic deformation zones) during sliding at 600–800°C.
generation.baseline: Conventional FeNiCrCoCu HEA coating without deliberate pre-oxidation treatment (minimal native oxide formation), subjected to identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted to occur under high-temperature sliding conditions (600–800°C) where the oxide layer is both formed and remains stable; at lower temperatures or in environments that do not favor oxide formation, the mechanism may not be active.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal oxide composition, thickness, and uniformity required for the protective effect are not fully defined, and the extent to which substrate interactions or alternate deformation modes contribute remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical metal substrates: one set receives a controlled pre-oxidation treatment to form the continuous oxide tribolayer, while the other is left untreated. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., using a ball-on-disk apparatus at 700°C) and characterize the wear volume, friction coefficient, and microscopic deformation (using SEM and TEM/EBSD analysis) of the coatings.
measurements: Wear volume and friction coefficient during sliding tests at 700°C
Microscopic deformation features and distribution of strain (via SEM, TEM, and EBSD)
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS or EDS) to confirm the presence and continuity of the oxide layers
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized coatings do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and more uniform microscopic deformation (or if they perform worse) compared to the untreated baseline under identical high-temperature sliding conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.
